title: Sukhmani close
hook: a psalm for peace in any week

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukhmani whole, and your line: the whole jewel. Today is the last of our hundred days with Sukhmani; tomorrow a new bani begins.

Some people keep one thing from a long trip. Not the whole suitcase of souvenirs; one thing. A smooth stone from a beach, a ticket stub, a recipe written on a napkin. Years later, holding it, the whole trip comes back: the light, the smells, who you were then. One small thing carries the rest. We've spent a hundred days walking through Sukhmani, from remembering to peace. At the close, the question is simple. What will you keep?
screen: `ONE STONE FROM A LONG TRIP.` → `ONE THING CARRIES THE REST.` → `WHAT WILL YOU KEEP?`

segments.voice: Sukhmani has been called a psalm of peace, and Sikhs turn to it in every kind of week: in a hospital waiting room, before an exam, at a new baby's welcome, on the anniversary of a death, and on ordinary Tuesdays when nothing in particular is wrong. That range is the point. Its peace isn't only for good weeks or only for bad ones. Look back at what we walked. Simran: remembering, and finding peace. The God-conscious person, humble as the earth. Honest pages on pride and slander and clever schemes. Wealth that stays behind, and kindness that travels. A wanderer at the door, a beggar asking for mercy. The stillness before creation, the Lord of every living thing, the eye-ointment of wisdom, the perfect One. And at the center, the line the whole bani grows from: the jewel of peace is the ambrosial Name. Nobody holds all of that at once. That's why today's practice is to keep one piece. Many Sikhs have a favorite stanza they know by heart and return to when they need it, like the stone from the beach: one piece that brings the whole back. Tomorrow we move to a new bani, Asa di Var, the ballad sung at dawn in gurdwaras, by Guru Nanak, with saloks by Guru Nanak and Guru Angad. It's a very different sound: bolder, sharper, written to a folk tune. But Sukhmani doesn't end because we've moved on. It's a circle, and whatever you keep from it, you can return to in any week.
screen: `A PSALM FOR EVERY KIND OF WEEK.` · `WHAT WE WALKED, FROM SIMRAN TO PEACE.` · `KEEP ONE PIECE, LIKE A STONE.` · `NEXT: THE BALLAD AT DAWN.` · then, large: `PEACE, KEPT.`

segments.voice: Let the last hundred days drift past: the beggar at the door, the stillness before creation, the eye-ointment, the earth that bears everything, the kindness that travels. Don't choose by thinking; notice which picture your mind keeps returning to, and hold it gently, like a stone in your palm. If you pray, rest in Waheguru with it.
Sukh, peace or ease: a psalm of peace for any week, we close our hundred days by keeping one piece of it, to bring the whole back when needed.
Your line: peace, kept. Thank you for walking all hundred of these days with me.

chat.says: Why read Sukhmani when nothing's wrong? Isn't it meant for hard times?
options: It's a psalm of peace for every kind of week: hard days, milestones and ordinary Tuesdays.
It's only for funerals and hospitals; reading it on a good day would bring bad luck.
It's only for priests to read; ordinary people should leave it to them.
